title: 2026-08-24 Verdant Logistics p95 & tokenflow discovery
summary: Discovery call to map Verdant Logistics' latency (p95) targets and token/sec bursting patterns across hosted, dedicated, and private deployment options. Discussed concurrency, streaming behavior, KV/prefix caching, and security constraints. Agreed next steps: run a tailored tokenflow benchmark, provide sample prompts, and share Dedicated pricing ranges.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
action_items: Priya Nair (SE): run 2 workload profiles (steady-state 250 rps, burst 2k rps) and share results - due 2026-08-31
Alex Kim (AE): send Dedicated pricing band and pilot terms - due 2026-08-26
Verdant (Maya): upload anonymized sample prompt set + traffic histogram - due 2026-08-28
next_steps: SE to run token/sec + p95 streaming benchmark using Verdant prompts
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark and sizing (30-45m) next week
AE to attach SOC 2 + security whitepaper and Dedicated SLA draft
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-24 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Lee (Verdant Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Verdant Director Infra), Samir Patel (Verdant Lead Eng)

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off in a minute. I'm Alex from Redwood, did folks get the invite ok?
[00:10] Maya Lee: Yeah thanks Alex, all good. We've got about an hour, we want to focus on p95 targets and how you handle token bursts especially with streaming responses.
[00:18] Alex Kim: Perfect, today Priya our SE is with me, she'll run through the perf/benchmark stuff. Priya do you want to orient?
[00:24] Priya Nair: Sure, hi team. Briefly we'll surface how Redwood routes requests across hosted/dedicated/private, how caching and batching affect p95, and then propose a tokenflow benchmark tailored to Verdant. We'll ask about sequence lengths, concurrent sessions, and burst profile.
[00:40] Tom Reynolds: To set context - our product generates dynamic route plans. Typical response lengths are 120-450 tokens, but we have a small subset of long reasoning prompts up to 2k tokens. We care about p95 user-facing latency under 400ms for short answers, and under 1.5s for the longer flows.
[00:58] Samir Patel: Our busiest windows see about 400 concurrent active sessions, but with bursts that can spike to ~2k concurrent for 60-90 seconds. Bursts are the main pain.
[01:10] Priya Nair: Got it. When you say concurrent sessions, is that concurrent streaming connections or discrete requests?
[01:16] Samir Patel: Mostly streaming websockets, yes. It's token-by-token UI streaming to clients. So tokens/sec during a burst is more meaningful than requests/sec.
[01:24] Priya Nair: That's helpful. Do you have a tokens/sec histogram or average seq length distribution we can use?
[01:31] Maya Lee: We have a histogram, yes. I'll anonymize and share. Average tokens/sec per stream during bursts is around 18-22 tokens/sec, but aggregate tokens/sec for the system hits ~40k-50k during spikes.
[01:45] Alex Kim: Ok, good. On Redwood side the key knobs are: batching window, prefix/K V caching, and model choice/quantization. For hosted we have pre-provisioned capacity and autoscaling, for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools so bursts are easier to absorb without scaling delays, and Private gives you total control but with ops overhead.
[02:05] Tom Reynolds: For security we need VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, audit logs and SOC 2 type 2. We'll also need proof of not storing PII beyond session retention windows.
[02:16] Alex Kim: We support VPC private deployments, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs. We can provide our SOC2 and ISO docs.
[02:23] Maya Lee: Cool. Cost is also a driver — we need an estimate of per-token cost in hosted vs Dedicated amortized under your recommendations.
[02:31] Alex Kim: We'll give a cost comparator after the benchmark. For Dedicated often the unit cost drops with utilization, but there's an up-front reserved commit.
[02:40] Priya Nair: If I can jump to p95: p95 is highly sensitive to tail variance driven by batching and kernel selection. For streaming low-latency tokens you want small batch windows and aggressive prefix/K V caching -- that reduces KV cache warmups. We also tune the model variant: e.g. a quantized variant for lower-latency short responses.
[02:59] Samir Patel: Quick question: how do you handle KV cache for multi-turn sessions across a cluster? We saw some vendors where cache misses blow up latency.
[03:07] Priya Nair: We maintain session placement affinity for the KV cache, and have a lightweight prefix cache for common token prefixes. There are cases where cross-node eviction causes a miss but for the workloads you described we can keep affinity for 80-90% of active sessions.
[03:20] Maya Lee: That sounds promising. During bursts our biggest issue is cold starts on scaling events, not necessarily steady-state.
[03:28] Priya Nair: For cold starts we have capacity tiers and fast failover to compatible model variants. For Dedicated you can reserve a buffer of machines for bursts — that avoids cold start scaling. In hosted we'd recommend a warm-burst policy or pinned instances.
[03:41] Tom Reynolds: Is there a quick rule of thumb you use to translate tokens/sec aggregate into Dedicated sizing?
[03:48] Priya Nair: A rough heuristic: pick your target p95 for short seqs (say 350ms), measure per-stream tokens/sec and average seq, and multiply by concurrency. We'll run a micro-benchmark; for example an A100-class Dedicated node can sustain X tokens/sec for model Y at p95 300-400ms — we'll provide specific numbers after we run with your prompts.
[04:10] Alex Kim: Note that the X varies by model and quantization — we'll run 2 profiles: one with canonical open model (we'll test 2 variants) and one with a lower-latency quantized variant.
[04:20] Maya Lee: We prefer open models for cost, but we'll consider Redwood-verified variants. Also what's your approach to throttling during system-wide overloads?
[04:29] Alex Kim: We provide graceful degradation: per-customer rate limiting, fallback to cheaper model variant, and region failover. For critical flows you can implement hedged requests or shorter completion lengths. We can include failover playbooks in the ops runbook.
[04:42] Samir Patel: During a previous vendor test we saw p95 jump from 300ms to 1.8s for about a minute during a 2k-concurrency burst — we need to avoid that.
[04:50] Priya Nair: Understood. Our benchmark will simulate your burst profile and measure p50/p95/p99, cold-start percentiles, and token/sec throughput. We'll also run streaming token-by-token latency traces.
[05:03] Maya Lee: Can you simulate our long sequences too? The 2k token flows are rare but latency-sensitive for planning updates.
[05:09] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll run two buckets: short (120-450 tokens) and long (1.5k-2k tokens). We'll measure end-to-end p95 and token emission latency.
[05:20] Tom Reynolds: For Private deployments, what's the expected operational work? Ops resources, monitoring integrations, etc?
[05:27] Alex Kim: On Private you'll get a customer-managed control plane; we provide the deployment artifacts and onboarding. Ops work includes capacity planning, kernel/driver compatibility, and regular updates. We offer an enterprise snapshot for the first quarter with Redwood-managed upgrades as an add-on.
[05:41] Maya Lee: Ok. In terms of metrics, besides p95 we'd want per-route token counts, per-token CPU/GPU cycles, and billing alignment to those metrics.
[05:50] Priya Nair: We can provide per-route breakdowns and token-level cost attribution in the Console. For the benchmark we'll produce a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates under projected utilization.
[06:02] Samir Patel: Any gotchas with VPC peering? Last vendor required peering and we had lots of NAT/egress config issues.
[06:09] Alex Kim: We typically do VPC peering or private link; we share a network checklist. For egress we can support private endpoints to avoid internet egress. We'll include that in the security pack.
[06:20] Maya Lee: Great. About SLAs — we need clarity on latency SLOs vs uptime. Can you share what you typically commit to for Dedicated?
[06:27] Alex Kim: For Dedicated we provide latency targets per model family and a throughput SLA; for example baseline p95 targets for common models are published, and we'll negotiate a customer-specific SLA tied to reserved capacity. We'll include examples in the follow-up.
[06:40] Tom Reynolds: What do your telemetry hooks look like? We have existing tracing and SRE pipelines.
[06:45] Priya Nair: We emit span-level traces, per-request metadata, and token-level timing. Integrations: Datadog, New Relic, Prometheus exporters. We also provide downloadable traces for internal benchmarking.
[06:58] Maya Lee: Awesome. Can you also show how you handle prompt transformations and safety checks inline? We sometimes rewrite prompts before sending.
[07:06] Priya Nair: We have pre-request hooks and server-side prompt filters; those run with minimal extra latency since they're executed before batching. We can include that in the test harness if you want.
[07:18] Alex Kim: Quick backlog question — do you need model version pinning for compliance?
[07:22] Maya Lee: Yes, for auditability we want version pinning and a changelog for model updates.
[07:27] Alex Kim: We support pinning and rollout policies.
[07:30] Samir Patel: Ok, on the benchmark specifics: can we ask Redwood to run a 12-hour soak test that includes three 2-minute burst windows per hour replicating our histogram plus a 15-minute long-seq stress at the end?
[07:42] Priya Nair: Yes, we can run that; we'd ask you to provide the exact traffic file and a test account. For hosted we'll run it in a sandbox tenant; for Dedicated we can provision a pilot set.
[07:55] Tom Reynolds: How long to get the pilot nodes? We could start with a small Dedicated footprint if the numbers look good.
[08:01] Alex Kim: We can provision pilot Dedicated nodes within 48-72 hours subject to contract, but for initial benchmark we can run in hosted with pinned capacity to emulate Dedicated.
[08:11] Maya Lee: That would work. For cost modeling we need amortized per-token price at 70% utilization and 90% utilization.
[08:19] Alex Kim: We'll include both scenarios.
[08:22] Priya Nair: One more technical note: streaming p95 is measured as token emission latency — that's different from overall completion latency. We'll capture both metrics since UX cares about the first emitted tokens and the continued tail.
[08:35] Samir Patel: Makes sense. Any constraints on the prompt content? We have some PII, so we'll need to redact unless we sign an NDA.
[08:43] Alex Kim: We can sign an NDA or you can anonymize the dataset — either works. For security review we can start with redacted prompts.
[08:52] Maya Lee: We'll redact and share the histogram.
[08:56] Alex Kim: Great. I'm going to quickly recap next steps — Priya you'll run the benchmark with the two profile variants and share a results workbook; Alex will send pricing, SOC2/security docs, and a pilot proposal; Verdant to share prompts and traffic histograms. Anything to add?
[09:12] Maya Lee: Include a runbook example for burst mitigation please.
[09:16] Alex Kim: Will do.
[09:18] Tom Reynolds: Also include Dedicated buffer sizing guidance for 2k-concurrency 90s bursts.
[09:24] Alex Kim: Noted.
[09:26] Priya Nair: I'll also include a sample curl/websocket harness and a short adapter for your tracing pipeline.
[09:33] Maya Lee: Thanks. That sounds like the right approach.
[09:36] Alex Kim: Ok we'll follow up with those artifacts and book a 30-45 minute review next week. Thanks all.
[09:41] Meeting end.
notes: Customer emphasized bursts and streaming tokens/sec as primary risk
Redwood to run both short/long seq benchmarks + streaming token emission latency traces
Security: VPC, KMS, SOC2 required; NDA for PII prompts suggested
